title: KV cache paging, telemetry, and burst recovery - Sunrise Health
summary: SE deep-dive with Sunrise Health on repeated KV cache evictions during high-burst patient-qa sessions. Discussed telemetry signals to detect saturation, paging/spill behavior, prefix reuse causing hot-set thrash, and mitigation strategies (adaptive batching, tiered prefix caching, eviction priority by recency vs product impact). Action items: Redwood to share compact telemetry dashboard, run a targeted replay test, and propose a pilot config for a dedicated pool + on-prem KMS integration.
action_items: Luca Chen (Redwood SE): Share example telemetry dashboard (KV hit rate, eviction rate, avg prefix reuse) - due 2025-09-10
Priya Singh (Sunrise): Provide 2 weeks of anonymized request traces and sample long-context sessions - due 2025-09-09
Maya Patel (AE): Schedule pilot kickoff for dedicated pool and on-prem tunnel - due 2025-09-12
Marco Diaz (Sunrise SRE): Run baseline load test using Redwood replay tool and attach logs - due 2025-09-15
next_steps: Redwood to send the telemetry dashboard link and a short README on KV metrics
Customer to upload traces to secure share (S3 link mentioned in chat)
Follow-up call next Tuesday to review replay results and pilot config
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-03
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Recording ID: ff-20250903-7c4b
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luca (Redwood SE), Daniel (CTO), Priya (Lead ML), Aisha (Infra), Marco (SRE)

[00:00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Today Luca and I want to walk through the KV cache behavior you're seeing — evictions, paging, and the long-context sessions you mentioned. Quick intro?
[00:00:12] Daniel: Hey, yeah this is Daniel. We're basically seeing these bursty patient Q&A loads where we'll get long histories, sometimes 8k-12k token contexts, and after about 10 minutes of peak traffic the LLM responses start slowing and error spikes.
[00:00:28] Priya: And to add, we notice requests that share prefixes seem to get faster early on then suddenly regress, like the cache is colding or something.
[00:00:36] Luca: Right, so two immediate suspects: prefix reuse causing hot-set saturation, and paging/eviction kicking in when the in-memory KV footprint exceeds the pool. We'll try to correlate with your telemetry.
[00:00:48] Aisha: One note — we're running in our VPC with on-prem connector. We have a dedicated Redwood trial cluster but haven't moved to Dedicated capacity yet. Also we have KMS in-house so any spill to storage needs to be encrypted.
[00:01:02] Maya: Good to know. Luca, do you wanna show the example KV metrics we've seen in other customers?
[00:01:07] Luca: Sure. I'm going to share a screen (describing). Typical metrics we look at: KV hit rate by prefix hash, eviction rate (evictions/min), paging events (spill to disk/min), avg KV size per request, and sequence length distribution. Also batching latency percentiles because batching increases the KV memory working set.
[00:01:30] [00:01:30] Speaker 1: (noise)
[00:01:32] Priya: Can you explain paging? Is that when the KV cache offloads to disk? We've seen references to "spillover" in the docs.
[00:01:39] Luca: Exactly. When the in-memory KV region hits capacity, the runtime either evicts entries or moves less-recent entries to a slower store (if configured). We call that paging/spill. It avoids immediate misses but increases latency for requests that touch the paged keys. And with long-context sessions, the KV footprint per session is larger so you get quicker spill.
[00:01:58] Marco: We're seeing correlated IO spikes when this happens, matches our EBS provisioned bursts — so maybe the paging is synchronous and causing head-of-line latency.
[00:02:07] Maya: That would explain the slowdown. Are you seeing drop in throughput before errors?
[00:02:12] Daniel: Yes throughput drops, then we start seeing token generation timeouts on some paths.
[00:02:18] Luca: A common pattern we measure: 1) prefix popularity concentrated in a small hot set, 2) KV fill ramps up during bursts, 3) eviction kicks in and thrashes between a few large prefixes, 4) paging causes increased p99 latency and eventually some request failures when upstream client retries saturate.
[00:02:37] Priya: How does prefix reuse play into eviction? We're intentionally using similar prompt scaffolds for many patients — so prefixes are reused a lot.
[00:02:44] Luca: Prefix reuse can be helpful because if the runtime can reuse KV entries across sessions it's a win. The problem is when you have many distinct prefixes that are all large — then reuse isn't enough and eviction prioritization matters.
[00:02:56] Aisha: Is eviction LRU? Can we change policy to be MRU or frequency based?
[00:03:01] Luca: The default is recency-weighted with a small frequency component — sort of a tiny-LFU/LRU hybrid. We can tune it per deployment: make eviction favor smaller entries, or prioritize by product impact tags you provide (you can mark prefixes as "pinned" for short windows).
[00:03:19] Daniel: Pinned sounds good but doesn't that increase memory?
[00:03:22] Luca: Yes, pinning increases memory use — so it's usually used for a small set of high-value prefixes. Alternatively we suggest tiered caches: keep a tiny hot-cache for the most frequent prefixes and a larger spillable region for the rest. That reduces thrash.
[00:03:36] [00:03:36] Speaker 2: uh-huh
[00:03:38] Priya: Any rules for what to pin? If we pin session templates that almost always reappear is that worth it?
[00:03:44] Luca: Yes, pinning templates or system prompts that are small and high-frequency is low-cost and high-benefit. Large per-user KV (like long conversation states) are harder to pin. For long conversations we recommend prefix compaction — summarize older tokens into a compacted prefix so the KV per session shrinks.
[00:04:01] Marco: Summarization will change semantics though. Are there guardrails?
[00:04:05] Maya: That's where evals come in. A compacted prefix can be tested against a prompt set to ensure no regression. Redwood Optimize can help automate that comparison.
[00:04:13] Priya: We also looked at quantization. We run some weights quantized on the model, but does quantization affect the KV size?
[00:04:21] Luca: Quantization primarily affects model weights and activation memory. For KV cache the main factor is the KV representation — 16-bit vs 8-bit vs packed formats. If the runtime uses compressed KV formats when quantized model artifacts are used, you can reduce per-entry size. That's an optimization we can enable; there are trade-offs in CPU decompress cost during lookup.
[00:04:40] Aisha: So compressed KV reduces memory but adds CPU latency on miss/hit?
[00:04:44] Luca: Correct. If your latency SLO is tight, decompression cost might be unacceptable at p99. The runtime can do on-path decompression only for paged entries to balance cost.
[00:04:54] Daniel: What about batching? We thought more batching reduces per-token cost but seems to increase memory.
[00:05:00] Luca: Yes batching increases the concurrent KV working set because you have to hold KV for multiple in-flight requests. Continuous batching is great for throughput but can push you past memory thresholds. We can recommend adaptive batching policies based on current memory pressure and sequence length distribution.
[00:05:15] Priya: Can Redwood runtime throttle batch size dynamically?
[00:05:18] Luca: Yes, we have adaptive batching controls. The policy can lower max batch size when eviction rate exceeds a threshold, or prioritize latency SLOs by reducing batch wait time.
[00:05:27] [00:05:27] Speaker 3: Okay
[00:05:28] Marco: How do we detect the root cause quickly? Our team is blind until we see latencies spike.
[00:05:33] Luca: Key telemetry signals: sudden drop in KV hit rate plus rising eviction rate, increase in paging events, p99 latency of token generation moving up correlated with IO ops. We suggest adding a composite alert that triggers when eviction_rate > X AND paging_events > Y AND p99_token_time increases by Z%.
[00:05:53] Priya: What X and Y are typical?
[00:05:56] Luca: Start conservatively: eviction_rate > 50/min and paging_events > 5/min for small clusters. We'll calibrate after seeing your trace.
[00:06:05] Maya: Also instrument prefix cardinality — number of active prefixes in the last 5m. High cardinality with high median size is a red flag.
[00:06:13] Daniel: We can add those metrics. On the topic of spill encryption — since we run in our VPC and want on-prem KMS, will spill-to-disk respect our KMS keys?
[00:06:22] Luca: Yes with Private deployment we can integrate with your KMS/HSM. For Hosted, Redwood encrypts at rest with customer-managed keys for Dedicated/Private. We'll need to validate the key exchange during pilot.
[00:06:34] Aisha: Any quick mitigations to get us through next week's expected load?
[00:06:38] Maya: Short-term fixes: reduce max_batch_size, enable a tiny pinned hot-cache for most frequent templates, lower KV TTL for non-critical prefixes, and increase the pool memory temporarily if possible. Also consider enabling nonblocking async paging if available so IO doesn't stall the inference thread.
[00:06:56] Priya: How fast can we get a config change?
[00:06:58] Maya: For Hosted trial we can push non-destructive runtime config changes in the next 24-48 hours. For Dedicated, changes are slightly slower but doable in a day.
[00:07:07] Marco: We want to reproduce locally. Is there a replay tool?
[00:07:11] Luca: Yes, we'll share the replay harness. It can simulate your sequence length distribution and prefix patterns. Best to run it against a staging instance with telemetry enabled.
[00:07:20] [00:07:20] Daniel: Can the replay simulate pinned vs non-pinned behavior?
[00:07:23] Luca: It can simulate prefix frequencies and sizes, which is enough to see eviction dynamics. Pinning is a runtime flag, we'll test both modes.
[00:07:30] Priya: Any concerns about data residency during replay if we upload traces?
[00:07:34] Maya: Use anonymized traces; Redwood's intake supports encrypted upload to your dedicated bucket or a temporary S3 link with SSE-KMS using your key.
[00:07:43] Aisha: You mentioned circuit breakers earlier — how do those work?
[00:07:46] Luca: Circuit breakers can limit incoming QPS to preserve overall SLOs. For example, when paging_events > threshold and p99>target, the controller can reject low-priority requests or route them to a cheaper, higher-latency fallback model. That prevents full outage.
[00:08:02] Daniel: We need to think about user-facing degradations. Graceful fallback is better than timeouts.
[00:08:05] Maya: Agreed; we can set up a canary fallback policy for patient Q&A: degrade to shorter context variant or synthetic summary fallback with an explanatory agent message.
[00:08:16] Priya: Do you have recommended defaults for TTL and eviction windows?
[00:08:20] Luca: Defaults depend on workload. For high-cardinality workloads keep TTL short (30-90s) and rely on prefix compaction. For low-cardinality, longer TTLs are fine. We'll suggest a starting config after we review traces.
[00:08:34] [00:08:34] Speaker 4: (crosstalk)
[00:08:35] Marco: If we go Dedicated what are the benefits re: KV?
[00:08:38] Luca: Dedicated gives you larger pools and predictable memory per slot, more control over eviction policies, and the ability to reserve higher memory instances so paging is less likely. Also you can enable local NVMe spill which is faster than network storage.
[00:08:52] Daniel: On-prem — can we host the entire runtime?
[00:08:55] Luca: With Redwood Private you can run the runtime in your VPC or on-prem. We ship the control plane as customer-managed and integrate with your KMS. There are operational trade-offs — you become responsible for node maintenance, but latency and data residency are best.
[00:09:09] Priya: Any gotchas for AWS Outposts or isolated racks?
[00:09:12] Luca: Ensure NVMe performance is predictable; also network egress between the controller and runtime must be low-latency. We'll validate during the pilot.
[00:09:20] Maya: Let's quickly recap action items and owners. Luca will share the telemetry dashboard and replay harness; Priya will upload traces; Maya will schedule the pilot; Marco will run baseline tests. Anything else?
[00:09:34] Daniel: Also send over a short doc on prefix compaction patterns and an example config for adaptive batching.
[00:09:40] Maya: We'll include that in the follow-up email. Thanks everyone.
[00:09:44] [00:09:44] End of meeting transcript summary notes: Key risk: hot-set saturation from prefix reuse leading to eviction/paging causing p99 latency spikes. Short-term mitigations recommended.
